title: The Journey to the Great Oz, part 3
attribution: From The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum (1900), via Project Gutenberg, in reading order.
body: The Scarecrow sat upon the Lion’s back, and the big beast walked to the edge of the gulf and crouched down.
“Why don’t you run and jump?” asked the Scarecrow.

“Because that isn’t the way we Lions do these things,” he replied. Then giving a great spring, he shot through the air and landed safely on the other side. They were all greatly pleased to see how easily he did it, and after the Scarecrow had got down from his back the Lion sprang across the ditch again.

Dorothy thought she would go next; so she took Toto in her arms and climbed on the Lion’s back, holding tightly to his mane with one hand. The next moment it seemed as if she were flying through the air; and then, before she had time to think about it, she was safe on the other side. The Lion went back a third time and got the Tin Woodman, and then they all sat down for a few moments to give the beast a chance to rest, for his great leaps had made his breath short, and he panted like a big dog that has been running too long.

They found the forest very thick on this side, and it looked dark and gloomy. After the Lion had rested they started along the road of yellow brick, silently wondering, each in his own mind, if ever they would come to the end of the woods and reach the bright sunshine again. To add to their discomfort, they soon heard strange noises in the depths of the forest, and the Lion whispered to them that it was in this part of the country that the Kalidahs lived.
“What are the Kalidahs?” asked the girl.

“They are monstrous beasts with bodies like bears and heads like tigers,” replied the Lion, “and with claws so long and sharp that they could tear me in two as easily as I could kill Toto. I’m terribly afraid of the Kalidahs.”

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why did the Lion not run before jumping?
options: That is not the way Lions do these things
The edge of the gulf was too crumbling
The Scarecrow would have fallen off
He had no room to take a run

questions.prompt: Per the passage, how many times did the Lion cross the ditch in all?
options: Three times over and back again
Once only, carrying all three
Twice, carrying two at a time
Four times, once for each of them

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did Dorothy hold on to as she crossed?
options: The Lion's mane
The Lion's collar
The Scarecrow's arm
Her own basket

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what are the Kalidahs like?
options: Bodies like bears and heads like tigers
Bodies like tigers and heads like bears
Bodies like lions and heads like wolves
Bodies like bears and heads like men

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who told them the Kalidahs lived there?
options: The Lion, in a whisper
The Tin Woodman, from his father
The Scarecrow, from the crows
Dorothy, from the Munchkins

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, how did the great leaps affect the Lion?
options: They left him short of breath and panting
They tore the claws on his front feet
They made him bolder than before
They left him unable to walk further

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what was on each traveller's mind after crossing?
options: Whether they would ever reach sunshine again
Whether the Lion could be trusted at all
Whether the Wizard would grant their wishes
Whether they had food enough for the day

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why is the Lion so afraid of the Kalidahs?
options: Their claws could tear him in two
They hunt in packs too large to fight
They cannot be frightened by any roar
They have hunted him once before

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does gloomy describe about the forest?
options: Dark and dispiriting
Thick with thorns
Full of loud noises
Damp underfoot

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the passage?
options: The ditch is crossed, but the forest ahead is darker and worse
The Lion refuses the jump and the party turns back
The travellers come out of the forest into sunshine
The Kalidahs attack while the party is crossing

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Lion do before springing?
options: Walked to the edge and crouched down
Took a long run at the gulf
Measured the gap with his paw
Roared to give himself courage

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did Dorothy carry across with her?
options: Toto, in her arms
The basket of nuts on her back
The oil-can in her pocket
Nothing at all

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how did the crossing feel to Dorothy?
options: As if she were flying through the air
As though the fall would never end
Slower than she had expected
Rougher than riding in a wagon

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did the party sit down after the third crossing?
options: To let the Lion get his breath back
To eat the nuts before going on
To wait for the noises to stop
To decide which way to go next

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, how does the Lion compare the Kalidahs' strength to his own?
options: They could tear him apart as easily as he could kill Toto
They are about as strong as he is himself
They are slower than he is but far heavier
They can only harm him if there are several

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does panted mean?
options: Breathed hard and quickly
Growled deep in his throat
Lay down and would not move
Shook his mane out

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarises the passage?
options: A crossing safely made, and a warning about what lives ahead
A crossing that costs the Lion the last of his strength
A meeting with the Kalidahs on the far side of the ditch
A decision to leave the road and go around the forest
